cases.context: Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: All households, businesses, quantities, prices, shocks and behavior below are fictional teaching assumptions. They are not descriptions of Huang, his family or any actual reaction to the public news.

After reading the affair-related headlines, a fictional household reviews the staffing and finances of its catering side business. Its decision to review the plan is stipulated for this exercise. The productivity, wage, price and staffing changes in the parts are separate hypothetical stress tests, not effects inferred from personal conduct or publicity.
A price-taking household catering business produces Y=A√(KN). Baseline A=4 and installed K=25 are fixed when it chooses labor N≥0. Output price P=1 and nominal wage W=5, so real wage w=W/P=5.
Inputs and output are divisible. There are no hiring costs. Unless a part specifies a capacity limit, labor is unrestricted. Capital receives MPK when both factor payments are requested.
Each part states its reset or changed stage. Numerical units are normalized teaching units, not money, employment or financial estimates for an actual business.
objectives: Derive hiring from MPN=w and separate movements from shifts.
Reconcile factor payments, real and nominal magnitudes, and capital stocks.
Test inverse inferences and a capacity/shutdown boundary.

The affair-related headlines prompt a fictional household to revisit its spending plan. This is an assumed planning exercise. The current-income bonus, future-income loss and payment delays below are independent hypothetical alternatives, not financial events involving Huang or his family.

A fictional household receives real income from freelance work at two dates. Baseline incomes are y₁=120 and y₂=80, initial assets and terminal bequests are zero, and borrowing/lending are unrestricted at the same gross real return R=2.

Preferences are U=√c₁+β√c₂ with β=1/2, unless a part explicitly asks to infer β. Thus the return is a deliberately large teaching calibration, not an observed market rate. Both consumptions are nonnegative.
Saving is s₁=y₁−c₁ and c₂=y₂+Rs₁. Each shock resets to the stated baseline; income news is assumed certain within the model.
objectives: Derive the Euler-budget solution and recognize rising, falling and flat profiles.
Keep current and future goods separate in MPCs and wealth comparisons.
Use observed allocations and responses to test whether one model can explain all evidence.

cases.title: Affair headlines and a household cash cushion
cases.context: Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: All households, businesses, quantities, prices, shocks and behavior below are fictional teaching assumptions. They are not descriptions of Huang, his family or any actual reaction to the public news.

After reading the affair-related headlines, a fictional household checks how it would fund current spending if income arrives later. Payment timing, income changes and borrowing limits are stipulated separately. The exercise makes no claim that the news actually changed anyone’s income or access to credit.
A fictional household supported by freelance earnings has U=ln c₁+.8ln c₂, incomes y₁=60 and y₂=150, no initial assets, no bequest, and gross real return R=1.25. Both consumptions must be positive.
Saving is s=y₁−c₁ and c₂=y₂+1.25s. Lending is unrestricted. A borrowing cap B means s≥−B, equivalently c₁≤y₁+B. Where allowed, borrowing and lending have the same return.

Unless reset, preferences and R stay fixed. No borrowing corresponds to B=0. Each payment advance is exactly offset by a stated future income reduction, so its financial value can be distinguished from its effect on access to cash.
objectives: Compare an unconstrained optimum with the credit ceiling before using Euler equality.
Identify thresholds, positive and zero wedges, and piecewise responses.
Explain why equal present wealth need not imply equal consumption under credit limits.
cases.focus: Credit limits and changing regimes

Following the affair-related headlines, a fictional household reviews its balance sheet and consumption plan. Every asset gain, loss, income revision and financing response below is independently stipulated for teaching. A fictional household initially has real financial assets 90 and debt 65, hence net assets a₀=25. Parts A and B are balance-sheet exercises. Parts C–H reset to a two-period optimization model.

In that model, U=ln c₁+.5ln c₂, baseline gross real return R=2, and labor incomes are y₁=50,y₂=100. The large return is a teaching calibration. All net initial assets earn R before period-1 consumption, as in Supplement 3A. There are no bequests.

Unless a part prohibits debt, borrowing and lending are unrestricted at the same R. Closing net assets are a₁=Ra₀+y₁−c₁; saving is s₁=a₁−a₀=y₁+(R−1)a₀−c₁. Revaluations occur before this interest period and are not saving flows.
objectives: Separate a balance-sheet revaluation, financing transaction and saving flow.
Analyze explicit asset gains and losses with and without borrowing.
Test whether present-value compensation and local rate neutrality survive boundaries and finite changes.

After reading the affair-related headlines, fictional reader Mira reviews her own work, leisure and borrowing plan. Wage offers, interest rates, taxes and grants in the comparisons are stipulated separately; the headlines do not establish changes in any of them.
Mira chooses consumption c₁,c₂ and leisure l₁,l₂ with U=ln c₁+ln l₁+0.5(ln c₂+ln l₂). Each date has h=12 hours, 0<lₜ≤12, and cₜ>0. Work is nₜ=12−lₜ.

The baseline has wages (w₁,w₂)=(2,6), gross real return R=2, no initial assets, no taxes and no other income. Borrowing and lending are unrestricted unless a part changes that rule. No terminal financial assets remain.

Dated budgets are c₁+s₁=w₁n₁+b−T₁ and c₂=w₂n₂+Rs₁, where a part may specify an exogenous current grant b or lump-sum tax T₁. Otherwise b=T₁=0. A grant has no repayment or offsetting future tax in this household’s budget.
Each part explicitly resets or supplies its starting state. Rates, wages or grants not named in a shock remain fixed.
objectives: Derive joint choices rather than treating labor income as fixed.
Distinguish interior equality from time and borrowing boundaries.
Separate tax-base changes from lump-sum wealth changes.

cases.title: Affair headlines and a household’s tax-planning questions
cases.context: Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: Every household, business, number, economic shock and response below is fictional. These are teaching assumptions, not claims about Huang, his family, their finances or actual reactions to the news.

The affair-related headlines prompt fictional reader Dana to review household financial resilience. She uses the following teaching economy to ask how purchase plans and the timing or incidence of taxes affect a household’s spending capacity. No actual government response to the news is asserted.
For A–E, a closed two-period economy has fixed Y₁=Y₂=400, R=1, government purchases G₁=G₂=100 and lump-sum taxes T₁=T₂=100 initially. There is no inherited government debt or terminal debt.

The representative household has U=ln C₁+ln C₂, no assets, and unrestricted borrowing/lending. Purchases provide no direct utility or productivity benefit in this exercise. Taxes finance the purchase path in present value. Initial consumption is 300 each date and initial private, public and national current saving are zero.
Use S_private=Y₁−T₁−C₁, S_public=T₁−G₁ and S_national=Y₁−C₁−G₁. The interest rate and pretax incomes are held fixed throughout the comparisons.

The A–E choices and all saving responses are desired plans evaluated at the stipulated fixed interest rate, before imposing aggregate goods-market or loanable-funds clearing. They do not describe a complete new closed-economy equilibrium at that unchanged rate.

F–H explicitly replace the representative household with a financing-constrained household. They supply their own incomes and utility; do not reuse the A–E equal-consumption rule. Every purchase and tax proposal is a hypothetical comparison, not a reported policy response to the affair-related news.
objectives: Keep purchases distinct from the timing of their taxes.
Compare temporary, future-only and permanent spending.
Track how tax incidence changes wealth and binding constraints.
cases.focus: A fictional reader’s household resources, tax timing and incidence

A fictional household runs an events-supply side business. After reading the affair-related headlines, its owners review hiring and investment plans. The later productivity, wage and tax changes are independent hypothetical assumptions, not consequences inferred from personal conduct.

The household’s competitive two-period events supplier begins with K₁=50, depreciation d=0.2 and gross return R=1.2. It buys J≥0 units of new capital at price 2 now; K₂=40+J. It cannot sell inherited survivors in period 1.

Baseline present-value profit is Π=12√N₁−3N₁−2J+[20√K₂+12√N₂−3N₂+1.6K₂]/1.2. The term 1.6K₂ is untaxed terminal resale after depreciation. Labor is hired freely at the given wages, and all choices are nonnegative.

If a part imposes output-revenue tax τ, only future produced output 20√K₂+12√N₂ is multiplied by 1−τ. Wages, purchases and resale are not deductible or taxed in this deliberately simple revenue-tax experiment.
Other parts change exactly the named technology coefficient, future wage or capacity bound. Reset to baseline whenever stated; these are hypothetical model changes.
objectives: Derive all three firm first-order conditions with correct dates.
Distinguish capital stock, gross additions and inherited survivors.
Check marginal inequalities when investment or capacity binds.

A fictional household runs a small photography side business. The affair-related headlines prompt its owners to review their own equipment plans. Resale prices, tax rules, credits and capacity limits below are independently stipulated scenarios, not observed consequences of the headlines.

The household’s two-period photography business has K₁=64, depreciation d=0.25, survivors 48, R=1.25 and new physical investment J≥0. Capital is its only variable input; future output is 24√K₂, so MPK₂=12/√K₂ and K₂=48+J.

The current purchase price is q₁=8. Baseline future resale price per surviving capital unit is q₂=8. The firm sells (1−d)K₂ at the end of date 2. Prices are real consumption-good units. Borrowing is unrestricted.
A future output-revenue tax τ applies only when specified, with purchase and resale untaxed. A current investment credit z reduces the purchase cost per newly purchased unit to 8−z. Baseline τ=z=0.
Use Π=−(8−z)J+[(1−τ)24√K₂+0.75q₂K₂]/1.25, apart from fixed profits. No capital ceiling applies unless a part supplies one. Each scenario is a hypothetical reset.
objectives: Derive user cost with unequal purchase and resale prices.
Separate a marginal incentive from total tax revenue.
Recognize zero investment, zero NPV and an unbounded objective.

cases.title: Affair headlines, a cash reserve and a bond
cases.context: Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: Every household, business, number, economic shock and response below is fictional. These are teaching assumptions, not claims about Huang, his family, their finances or actual reactions to the news.

After reading the affair-related headlines, a fictional household reviews its cash reserve and a fixed-payoff bond. Aggregate price-clearing comparisons use the teaching economy below. Any inflation-expectation or liquidity-preference shift is a separate hypothetical assumption, not evidence of an actual response to the headlines.

Use a closed teaching economy for aggregate money-demand comparisons; it is separate from the household’s individual bond calculation. Baseline real output is Y=600, real rate r=0.04, anticipated inflation πᵉ=0.02 and nominal money M=1160. Money earns zero interest.

Real money demand is L=400+0.5Y−2000i+D, where D is a liquidity-preference shift initially zero. For this demand model use the course approximation i=r+πᵉ. Money-market clearing is M/P=L, with positive P and L.
In flexible-price comparisons hold r and Y fixed unless explicitly changed. In fixed-price comparisons allow the stated alternative variable to adjust. Do not impose both closures at once.

A separate zero-coupon bond is bought initially for 100 and pays a certain nominal 106 at maturity. Contracted payoff does not change with news. For realized bond returns use the exact inflation adjustment, not the approximate demand-model Fisher relation.

The case does not infer inflation, money demand, bond values or anyone’s finances from the public acknowledgement. Each economic shock below is explicitly hypothetical; the acknowledgement alone does not identify an economic effect.
objectives: Distinguish fixed-real-rate price clearing from fixed-price interest clearing.
Separate a holder’s realized return from a new buyer’s quoted yield.
Infer hidden expectations and liquidity shifts from jointly supplied observations.

cases.title: Do affair headlines explain an economic cycle?
cases.context: Huang publicly acknowledged infidelity in November 2026.
scenario: Every household, business, number, economic shock and response below is fictional. These are teaching assumptions, not claims about Huang, his family, their finances or actual reactions to the news.

Prompted by the affair-related headlines, a fictional reader asks whether an activity dashboard could establish an economic reaction. The invented quarterly data below have no calendar mapping to the real news. They support the stated descriptive comparisons, not a claim that the acknowledgement caused a cycle.

A regional activity index Y at quarters t=0,…,8 is [100,102,105,103,101,104,108,107,109]. Use it as the specified activity proxy, not as sufficient evidence for an official economy-wide recession declaration.

The baseline trend is Tₜ=100+t. Unless a part changes it, the absolute cycle gap is Yₜ−Tₜ. A strict interior peak exceeds both adjacent observations; a strict trough is below both. Endpoints do not establish turning points.
Nominal money stocks at t=0,…,8 are [200,204,214,230,235,238,250,270,275]. Quarter-t money growth is 100(Mₜ/Mₜ₋₁−1). Compare corresponding turning points in growth, not in the stock.
An unemployment indicator at t=0,…,8 is [6,5.5,5,5.2,6,5.5,4.8,5,4.6]. These are illustrative percentage rates. A part may provide an investment index or price index for a specific comparison.

Each part uses the original data unless it explicitly introduces a revision or a different trend. A growth-phase expansion means rising activity; a positive or negative gap is a separate trend comparison.
objectives: Compute the correct variable before classifying its direction and timing.
Keep real growth, nominal growth and trend position distinct.
Reassess turning points under revisions and strict boundary requirements.

cases.title: When the price level finishes adjusting
cases.context: US midterms elect the House of Representatives and roughly one third of the Senate.
scenario: All numerical values, policy choices and behavioral changes below are hypothetical teaching assumptions, not estimates of US policy or economic effects.
The reduced-form goods equation is r=a−0.1Y, and real money demand is L=2Y−10r. Nominal M is positive. Interest rates and a use percentage-point units. Initially a=15,M=300,Y*=100 and P=2.

For an explicitly stated fixed-price stage, P stays at its initial value and IS–LM determines output. For a full-adjustment stage, output equals the stated Y* and P clears money. Expected inflation and money-demand behavior are otherwise unchanged.

Except where a part changes capacity, Y*=100 is fixed. Each monetary or fiscal proposal is a separate hypothetical experiment. Changes in a are net goods-demand shifts, already incorporating any stated financing effects.

cases.title: Two labor markets evaluate the same proposal
cases.context: US midterms elect the House of Representatives and roughly one third of the Senate.
scenario: All numerical values, policy choices and behavioral changes below are hypothetical teaching assumptions, not estimates of US policy or economic effects.

Workers are divisible. Production is Y=20N−N²/2, with marginal product 20−N on the economically relevant range 0≤N≤20. In the competitive economy labor demand is Nᵈ=20−w and initial supply is Nˢ=2w−4, where w is real pay.

A second economy has the same production function but maintains an efficiency wage w=10. It hires the lesser of desired labor Nᵈ and available labor Nˢ. Its effort schedule and wage rule remain fixed unless explicitly changed.
Where goods and assets are used, IS is r=a−0.1Y with initial a=30, money demand is L=Y−5r and M=300. Rates are percentage points. Full adjustment uses each economy’s own capacity output.

A hypothetical tax-financed purchase proposal is represented by two stated reduced-form shifts, supply changing to Nˢ=2w+2 and a rising to 32. Other parts specify separate resets. These are illustrative assumptions rather than a universal quantified fiscal response.
objectives: Explain how labor-market assumptions change fiscal capacity effects
Follow each capacity result through goods and money equilibrium
Identify when worker availability becomes a binding constraint

cases.title: Announcements, surprises and offsetting news
cases.context: US midterms elect the House of Representatives and roughly one third of the Senate.
scenario: All numerical values, policy choices and behavioral changes below are hypothetical teaching assumptions, not estimates of US policy or economic effects.

The hypothetical economy has surprise supply Y=100+25(P−Pᵉ), with price levels rather than log prices in this equation. Goods equilibrium is r=a−0.08Y and real money demand is L=Y−5r. Rates and a use percentage-point units.
Initially a=14,M=140 and P=Pᵉ=2. Real capacity remains Y*=100. In an unexpected experiment, Pᵉ initially stays at its pre-announcement value. With fully correct expectations, P=Pᵉ and Y=100.

cases.title: Hiring after a procurement opportunity
cases.context: US midterms elect the House of Representatives and roughly one third of the Senate.
scenario: All numerical values, policy choices and behavioral changes below are hypothetical teaching assumptions, not estimates of US policy or economic effects.

A hypothetical contractor can pay a real wage w>0. Effort is e(w)=w²/(9+w²), effective labor is E=e(w)N, output is Y=24A√E, and operating profit is Y−wN. Workers are divisible and output is sold at a normalized real price of one.
Initially A=1 and enough workers are available. Except for explicitly stated restrictions, both wage and headcount can be chosen. The no-operation choice has zero operating profit.

Some parts separately impose a wage floor, a headcount cap or a discrete wage set. A final part stipulates a fixed administrative cost of resetting nominal pay, using the same net-gain logic as the lecture’s reset-cost comparison. These restrictions are original teaching assumptions.
objectives: Derive the optimal effort-adjusted wage and actual headcount
Check when wage or labor constraints replace the interior conditions

cases.title: Should a supplier change its posted price
cases.context: US midterms elect the House of Representatives and roughly one third of the Senate.
scenario: All numerical values, policy choices and behavioral changes below are hypothetical teaching assumptions, not estimates of US policy or economic effects.

A hypothetical supplier faces orders Q=max((a−P)/0.5,0), where P is its selling price. It has constant real marginal cost c, no fixed operating cost and enough production capacity. At any posted price it may sell the demanded amount or choose zero production.
Initially a=20,c=4 and the posted price is P=12. Resetting its price costs F=18 once; keeping its old price or producing nothing incurs no reset cost. A reset can choose any nonnegative price.

If net profits tie, the manager retains the old price. Each part is a separate experiment unless it specifies otherwise. The demand and cost changes are hypothetical responses to possible policy conditions, not measured US effects.
objectives: Distinguish frictionless markup from a profitable price reset
Compare positive and negative shocks when the zero-orders boundary matters
Infer adjustment-cost thresholds from observed decisions

cases.title: Targets when the unemployment benchmark moves
cases.context: US midterms elect the House of Representatives and roughly one third of the Senate.
scenario: All numerical values, policy choices and behavioral changes below are hypothetical teaching assumptions, not estimates of US policy or economic effects.

Use p=ln(P). Inflation π is measured in 100 log-point units, and unemployment u is in percentage points. Initially Y*=100,u*=5 and Y−Y*=1000(p−pᵉ). The output-unemployment relation is Y−Y*=−4(u−u*). Expected inflation is initially 2.

Actual and expected inflation share the same previous-price baseline, so π−πᵉ=100(p−pᵉ). Demand policy can change actual unemployment, while a supply or structural change may change Y*,u* or the price-surprise coefficient only when explicitly stated.

Each part resets to the baseline unless it explicitly supplies new parameters. Probability distributions, persistence rules and uncertainty intervals are original hypothetical illustrations. They are not estimated US relationships or guaranteed policy effects.
objectives: Derive the Phillips coefficient with consistent units
Distinguish changed expectations, actual outcomes and natural benchmarks
Solve inverse and robust targets while respecting expectation adjustment

questions.prompt: Baseline: A=4, K=25 and w=5. What are profit-maximizing employment, output and the labor bill (N,Y,wN)?

choices.feedback: For positive A and K, marginal product is arbitrarily high near zero; some hiring is profitable.
MPN=10/√N equals 5 at N=4; production and the wage bill then follow.
This halves the correct employment; MPN at N=2 still exceeds the wage.
The wage bill is wN=5×4, not total output.
This sets average product, rather than marginal product, equal to the wage.
Installed capital need not equal employment, and marginal profit is negative at this employment.

questions.explanation: Y=20√N, so real operating surplus is 20√N−5N. Its derivative 10/√N−5 is zero at √N=2, and its second derivative is negative. Thus N=4, Y=40 and wN=20. This surplus is before capital payment.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations.

questions.prompt: Reset to baseline K=25 and w=5, then raise A alone from 4 to 5. After the catering business reoptimizes labor, what are N and the percentage change in Y from its baseline 40?

choices.feedback: The new output is 62.5; its gain relative to 40 is 22.5/40.

choices.text: N=3.2; Y is unchanged.
choices.feedback: A productivity rise raises labor demand at a fixed real wage.
The productivity gain raises output directly and induces hiring, so output rises more than 25%.

choices.text: N=4; Y rises 25%.
choices.feedback: This holds employment fixed even though the firm is allowed to reoptimize.

choices.text: N=5; Y rises 25%.
choices.feedback: Employment scales with A squared in this demand function, not linearly.

choices.text: N=6.25; Y rises 25%.
choices.feedback: This gets hiring right but omits the induced-employment output gain.

questions.explanation: MPN=12.5/√N=5 gives √N=2.5 and N=6.25. Output becomes 5√(25×6.25)=62.5. The increase is (62.5−40)/40=0.5625. The old labor-demand schedule has shifted, not merely been traversed.
questions.source: Tutorial 1 QP, PDF p1(a)–(g); Tutorial 1 ANS, PDF pp1–4. Original hypothetical extension using those production and factor-payment equations.

questions.prompt: New reset: raise A from 4 to 5 and w from 5 to 6.25 together, keeping K=25. Relative to baseline (N,Y)=(4,40), which result and explanation are correct?

choices.text: N falls to 2.56 and Y to 40.
choices.feedback: That is the wage-only hiring response evaluated while overlooking the productivity gain.

choices.text: N stays 4 and Y rises to 62.5.
choices.feedback: At N=4, the production function gives 5√100=50.

choices.text: N rises 25% and Y rises 50%.
choices.feedback: Employment depends on the ratio A/w squared; that ratio has not changed.

choices.text: N stays 4 and Y rises to 50: A/w is unchanged, but technology still raises output at that employment.
choices.feedback: Offsetting hiring incentives do not imply that production itself stays unchanged.

choices.text: N and Y both stay unchanged.
choices.feedback: Constant A/w preserves the hiring optimum, not the productivity multiplier in Y.

choices.text: c₁=80+x and s=−20 for every x.
choices.feedback: Beyond x=20 this exceeds the unchanged unconstrained target and no longer maximizes utility.

choices.text: c₁=80 and s=x−20 for every x.
choices.feedback: At first the binding cap moves with the advance, allowing consumption to rise.

choices.text: For x≤20, c₁=80+x; above 20, c₁=100; saving is zero throughout.
choices.feedback: The consumer borrows 20 in the first region and still borrows in the second until x=40.

choices.text: The switch occurs at x=40 because that is the original unconstrained borrowing need.
choices.feedback: The existing cap already provides 20, so only an additional 20 current units are needed to reach c₁=100.

choices.text: For 0≤x≤20, c₁=80+x and s=−20. For 20≤x≤40, c₁=100 and s=x−40.
choices.feedback: The advance initially raises a binding current ceiling; after it reaches the target, further advances reduce debt instead.

choices.text: c₁=100 and s=x−40 for every x.
choices.feedback: At x<20 that current consumption would breach the borrowing cap.

questions.explanation: PV wealth is (60+x)+(150−1.25x)/1.25=180. The unconstrained target remains 180/1.8=100. The credit ceiling is y₁+B=80+x, so c₁=min(100,80+x). For x≤20, saving is (60+x)−(80+x)=−20. For x≥20, it is 60+x−100=x−40. Future consumption is respectively 125−1.25x and 100. The formulas agree at x=20; the constraint has zero wedge there and is slack for larger x.

choices.text: Assets=110, debt=85 and net worth=25.

choices.text: Saving=3; assets=83, debt=55 and net worth=28.

choices.text: Saving=15; assets=93, debt=55 and net worth=38.

choices.text: Saving=25; assets=83, debt=55 and net worth=28.

questions.prompt: Optimization baseline: a₀=25, R=2, incomes (50,100), U=ln c₁+.5ln c₂, unrestricted credit. Initial assets earn interest before c₁. Which consumption, closing-assets and saving combination is correct?

choices.feedback: This exceeds present-value resources and cannot finance the stated future consumption.

choices.text: c₁=c₂=100, a₁=0 and s₁=−25.
choices.feedback: The household consumes all its initial principal by period end; zero closing assets do not mean zero saving.

choices.text: c₁=c₂=100, a₁=0 and s₁=0.
choices.feedback: Saving is the change from entering assets 25 to closing assets zero.
This treats initial assets as arriving at the consumption date and omits their first interest payment.

choices.text: c₁=c₂=100, a₁=−50 and s₁=−50.
choices.feedback: This uses labor income alone and omits both the inherited principal and its interest.
The budget is feasible, but βR=1 requires equal consumption at an unconstrained optimum.

questions.explanation: Current resources before consumption are Ra₀+y₁=2×25+50=100. Lifetime present wealth is 100+100/2=150. Log utility gives c₁=W/(1+.5)=100 and c₂=βR c₁=100. Closing assets are 100−100=0. Saving is a₁−a₀=−25, also 50+25 interest−100 consumption. Principal drawdown is distinct from a borrowing position.

questions.prompt: Reset to that optimization baseline, then impose a hypothetical pre-interest asset loss of 10, reducing a₀ from 25 to 15. Keep incomes, R=2 and credit access fixed. Which new closing assets and change in saving follow?

choices.feedback: The asset loss first removes 20 current resources because it occurs before gross interest accrues.
The household borrows after the loss; closing assets are negative.

choices.text: a₁=−20/3 and Δs₁=+10/3, even though consumption falls by 40/3 at each date.
choices.feedback: The loss reduces current interest income by 10 but reduces consumption by 40/3, making saving less negative.
Saving changes by the income effect minus the consumption change: −10−(−40/3)=+10/3.

choices.text: a₁=0 and Δs₁=+10.
choices.feedback: That imposes a no-debt constraint absent from this part.

choices.text: a₁=−10 and Δs₁=0.
choices.feedback: Current consumption adjusts through the wealth effect; it is not fixed at its baseline value.

questions.explanation: New wealth is 2×15+50+100/2=130, so c₁=c₂=130/1.5=260/3. The decline from 100 is 40/3. Closing assets are 30+50−260/3=−20/3. Saving is a₁−15=−65/3, compared with baseline −25=−75/3, so Δs₁=10/3. A wealth loss can reduce consumption and make the saving flow less negative while worsening the net asset position.
questions.source: Tutorial 4 QP, PDF p1, Question 1; Tutorial 4 ANS, PDF pp1–2. Original application of dated consumption, initial wealth and interest timing.

questions.prompt: Separate hypothetical asset-gain reset: a₀ rises from 25 to 35 before interest, with baseline incomes, R=2 and unrestricted credit. What happens to consumption, closing assets and saving?

choices.text: Each consumption rises by 40/3 and saving rises by 10/3.
choices.feedback: Extra interest income is 10, less than the 40/3 consumption increase, so saving falls.

choices.text: Each consumption rises by 40/3 and closing assets become −20/3.
choices.feedback: Current resources rise by 20 and consumption by only 40/3, leaving a positive closing balance.

choices.text: Each consumption rises by 20 and closing assets stay zero.
choices.feedback: This consumes the entire current resource gain and fails the unchanged Euler-budget solution.

choices.text: Each consumption rises by 40/3, closing assets rise to 20/3, and saving falls by 10/3.
choices.feedback: The household retains some of the larger principal while its consumption gain exceeds its extra interest income.

choices.text: Each consumption rises by 20/3, closing assets rise to 40/3, and saving rises.
choices.feedback: The pre-interest gain adds 20, not 10, to present consumption-date resources.

choices.text: Consumption does not change; all 10 extra assets remain saved.
choices.feedback: With normal dated consumption, the increase in lifetime wealth raises consumption at both dates.

questions.explanation: Present wealth is 2×35+50+100/2=170, so c₁=c₂=340/3. Each rises by 40/3. Closing assets are 70+50−340/3=20/3. Saving is 20/3−35=−85/3, a change of −10/3 from −75/3. Equivalently, Δs₁=(R−1)Δa₀−Δc₁=10−40/3. The positive gain and the negative-loss case are both explicit applications of the same fixed-rate linear budget response.

questions.prompt: Reset to the loss state a₀=15, incomes (50,100), R=2 and log weight .5. Now prohibit negative closing assets a₁<0. Which optimum and saving flow are correct?

choices.feedback: Closing assets zero do not imply a zero change from initial assets 15.
The household is allowed to spend existing principal and interest; it is not limited to labor income.

choices.text: c₁=80,c₂=100,a₁=0,s₁=−15; Euler equality holds.
choices.feedback: At this corner, 1/80−1/100 is positive, so the equality is replaced by a constraint wedge.
That allocation also violates a₁≥0 and is not the constrained optimum.

choices.text: c₁=80,c₂=100,a₁=0,s₁=−15; the debt constraint has a positive marginal value.
choices.feedback: Current resources cap consumption at 80, below the unconstrained target 260/3.
This is the unconstrained optimum and violates the new no-debt restriction.

questions.explanation: Current available resources are 2×15+50=80, so a₁≥0 requires c₁≤80. The unconstrained target is 260/3>80, so c₁=80 and a₁=0. Future consumption equals income 100. Saving is 0−15=−15. At the corner, the marginal gain from relaxing current consumption along the budget is 1/80−(.5×2)/100=1/400>0.
questions.source: Tutorial 4 QP, PDF p1, Question 1; Tutorial 4 ANS, PDF pp1–2. Original application of dated consumption, initial wealth and interest timing. Borrowing-boundary logic: Lecture 3 part 1, borrowing constraints.

questions.prompt: Compensation experiment: relative to baseline a₀=25,y₁=50,y₂=100,R=2, lose 10 initial assets but receive an additional 40 future income. This preserves present wealth 150. Compare unrestricted credit with a rule a₁≥0. Which pair of outcomes is correct?

choices.text: Both regimes give (100,100,−20).
choices.feedback: The second regime explicitly forbids the required negative closing assets.

choices.text: Both regimes give (80,140,0).
choices.feedback: The unconstrained household can borrow 20 to achieve its preferred flat profile.

choices.feedback: At a₀=15 and y₁=50, consuming 100 requires current borrowing of 20.

choices.text: Unrestricted gives (120,60,−40); no debt gives (80,140,0).
choices.feedback: The unrestricted allocation is feasible but fails βR=1, which requires equal consumption.

choices.text: The future gain cannot offset the loss even with credit because 40 and 10 differ.
choices.feedback: The initial loss removes 2×10=20 current resources; 40 future units have present value 20.

questions.explanation: After the changes, a₀=15 and y₂=140. Present wealth is 2×15+50+140/2=150, the baseline amount. Unrestricted log utility therefore gives c₁=c₂=100. Current resources are only 80, so a₁=80−100=−20 and future consumption checks as 140+2(−20)=100. If a₁≥0, the ceiling c₁≤80 binds; then c₁=80,c₂=140. PV equivalence and financing feasibility are separate requirements.

questions.prompt: Rate experiment reset: a₀=25, incomes (50,100), log weight .5 and unrestricted credit. Let R vary, retaining the rule that a₀ earns R before current consumption. At R=2, c₁=100 and its local derivative in R is zero. What happens in the two separate finite experiments R=1 and R=4?

choices.text: Both give c₁=350/3, but c₂ is 175/3 at R=1 and 700/3 at R=4; the local zero is a minimum, not global rate neutrality.
choices.feedback: The initial-asset and discounted-future-income effects cancel locally at R=2 but not over a finite change.

choices.text: Both leave c₁=100 because the derivative at R=2 is zero.
choices.feedback: A zero local derivative does not imply a constant function across finite rate changes.

choices.text: R=1 lowers c₁ to 250/3, while R=4 raises it to 350/3.
choices.feedback: At R=1, future income has larger present value, making total wealth 175 rather than 125.

choices.text: Both give c₁=c₂=350/3.
choices.feedback: The Euler ratio is c₂/c₁=βR, equal to .5 at R=1 and 2 at R=4.

choices.text: Both give c₁=350/3, proving the two lifetime allocations and welfare are identical.
choices.feedback: Future consumption differs by a factor of four; equal current consumption does not identify the whole allocation.

choices.text: Both give c₁=100 because the budget pivots around the same income endowment.
choices.feedback: Initial assets earn a rate-dependent amount before consumption, so that fixed-income-only pivot argument does not apply.

questions.explanation: Present wealth is W(R)=25R+50+100/R, and c₁=W/1.5. Its derivative is [25−100/R²]/1.5, zero at R=2 and increasing through zero there; its second derivative is 200/(1.5R³)>0. W(1)=W(4)=175, giving c₁=350/3 at either return. Euler gives c₂=.5R c₁: 175/3 at R=1 and 700/3 at R=4. A finite rate cut and rise can both raise current consumption around this minimum because initial wealth has its own timing effect.
questions.source: Tutorial 4 QP, PDF p1, Question 1; Tutorial 4 ANS, PDF pp1–2. Original application of dated consumption, initial wealth and interest timing.

questions.prompt: Mira’s baseline: wages are (2,6), R=2 and h=12. Which full-income budget and interior Euler ratio follow from the stated utility?

choices.text: The budget equals 60, and c₂/c₁=0.25.

choices.text: c₁+c₂/2=60, with no leisure terms, and c₂=c₁.

questions.prompt: Reset to baseline, then raise only current wage from 2 to 3. Both optima are interior. Which change in current work and saving is correct?

questions.prompt: Reset to w₁=2 and R=2. Let future wage w₂ increase from 6. At what w₂ does the interior candidate first reach zero current work, and what does a still larger wage imply for that candidate?

choices.text: There is no threshold because borrowing allows negative labor.
choices.feedback: Borrowing relaxes financing, not the physical bound l₁≤12.

choices.text: At w₂=8; above it the worker must retain the old consumption allocation.
choices.feedback: Consumption and future leisure must be reoptimized when the active constraint changes.

choices.text: At w₂=4; above it future leisure must be zero.
choices.feedback: Future leisure remains positive under log utility, and the current-time boundary occurs at 8.

choices.text: At w₂=8; above 8 the interior candidate requires l₁>12 and must be replaced by a boundary solution.
choices.feedback: The interior formula is l₁=4+w₂. It reaches the time endowment at 8.

choices.text: At w₂=6; every future-wage increase starts from zero current work.
choices.feedback: At w₂=6 the baseline has l₁=10 and current work 2.

choices.text: At w₂=12; only equality of wage and hours matters.
choices.feedback: Wages and hours are different units. The boundary follows from the allocation and budget.

questions.prompt: New state: w₁=2, w₂=10, R=2, no assets or transfers, unrestricted borrowing. The unconstrained interior candidate violates l₁≤12. Which actual allocation and boundary test are correct?

choices.text: l₁=12, c₁=c₂=30 and s₁=+30.
choices.feedback: With zero current income, positive consumption requires negative saving.

choices.text: l₁=12, c₁=c₂=30, but the boundary fails because Euler must fail at every corner.
choices.feedback: Only the current-leisure condition is at a boundary. Saving is unrestricted, so consumption Euler still holds.

choices.text: l₁=12, c₁=c₂=30, l₂=3 and s₁=−30; the net derivative toward more current leisure is 1/60>0.
choices.feedback: At no current work, the remaining present-value resources are 120/2=60. Reoptimization gives consumption 30 and future leisure 3.

choices.text: l₁=12, c₁=c₂=28, l₂=2.8 and s₁=−28.
choices.feedback: These keep the infeasible interior expenditure shares after clipping leisure. They leave resources unallocated.

choices.text: l₁=14, c₁=c₂=28 and l₂=2.8.
choices.feedback: The candidate has two more leisure hours than the physical endowment.

choices.text: l₁=12 and c₁=0 because there are no current earnings.
choices.feedback: Borrowing is unrestricted, so future earnings can finance current consumption.

Current saving is −30; future work earns 10(9)=90 and repays 60, leaving c₂=30. Holding c₁,l₂ fixed in the substituted objective, the current-leisure derivative is 1/12−βRw₁/c₂=1/12−2/30=1/60. A positive derivative at the upper leisure bound is consistent with optimality.

questions.prompt: Keep the new wages (2,10) and R=2, but now impose s₁≥0 with no assets or grants. Which allocation satisfies the borrowing boundary and both within-date leisure conditions?

choices.text: s₁=0 and c₁=c₂=36 because Euler always requires equality.
choices.feedback: Euler equality does not apply at a binding borrowing limit; c₁=36 cannot be financed by the proposed current allocation.

choices.text: s₁=0, l₁=l₂=6, c₁=12 and c₂=60.
choices.feedback: With no intertemporal transfer at the binding bound, each date splits its own full income equally between consumption and leisure expenditure.

choices.text: s₁=0, l₁=l₂=6, c₁=c₂=12.
choices.feedback: Future earnings are 10×6=60 and cannot be discarded in a monotone utility optimum.
This is the unrestricted solution and violates the new financing rule.

choices.text: s₁=0, l₁=12, c₁=0 and c₂=60.
choices.feedback: Zero current consumption gives log utility negative infinity and is dominated by working some current hours.

choices.text: s₁=0, l₁=l₂=6, c₁=60 and c₂=12.
choices.feedback: Those consumption amounts reverse the available dated earnings.

questions.explanation: At s₁=0, each date solves ln cₜ+ln lₜ subject to cₜ=wₜ(12−lₜ). Its interior leisure condition gives cₜ=wₜlₜ, so lₜ=6. Therefore c₁=12 and c₂=60. The feasible saving derivative is βR/c₂−1/c₁=1/60−1/12=−1/15<0. Saving more would lower utility, while the desired borrowing direction is prohibited.

questions.prompt: Reset to baseline wages (2,6), R=2 and unrestricted borrowing. Compare alternative taxes: A charges a current lump-sum tax of 12; B taxes current labor earnings at 50% with no lump-sum tax. Neither has an offsetting future tax change. Which current work and revenue comparison is correct?

choices.text: A induces 4 work hours and collects 12; B induces zero current work and collects zero.
choices.feedback: The lump-sum tax changes wealth at the original wage. The earnings tax lowers the net current wage to one and changes the chosen tax base.

choices.text: Both collect 12 because the 50% tax applies to 24 units of full labor income.
choices.feedback: The earnings tax applies to actual work, not to all 12 available hours.

choices.text: A induces zero work; B induces 4 hours.
choices.feedback: This reverses the wealth-only tax and the net-wage distortion.

choices.text: Both induce 4 hours because both reduce disposable income.
choices.feedback: Only B changes the price of leisure. The household must reoptimize its work and tax base.

choices.text: A induces 4 hours, so its saving is −8.
choices.feedback: That subtracts consumption from gross earnings without subtracting the lump-sum tax. Its actual saving is −20.

choices.text: B induces −4 current work hours and negative revenue.

Its interior l₁=16 exceeds 12, so current work is zero; reoptimizing at that corner gives c₁=18 and l₂=3. Tax revenue is 0.5×2×0=0. These are not equal-revenue policies.

questions.prompt: Start from the unrestricted no-current-work state with wages (2,10) and R=2. Raise only R. At what critical return does the current no-work corner just cease to have a positive upper-bound leisure derivative, and what are n₁ and s₁ at R=3?

choices.text: Critical R=2.5; at R=3 saving is +56/3.
choices.feedback: Current earnings are only 8/3 while consumption is 64/3; the resulting saving is negative.

choices.text: Critical R=5; at R=3 current work remains zero.
choices.feedback: The threshold includes 1+2β=2 as well as w₁ and R.

choices.text: Critical R=2; at R=3 n₁=4.
choices.feedback: The state at R=2 is strictly at the no-work corner, and the new full income must be discounted at 3.

choices.text: There is no release because wages do not change.
choices.feedback: R changes the intertemporal reward Rw₁/w₂ and the present value of future full income.

choices.text: Critical R=2.5; at R=3 c₁=c₂=64/3.
choices.feedback: Euler now gives c₂/c₁=βR=1.5, so c₂=32 rather than 64/3.

choices.text: Critical R=2.5; at R=3, n₁=4/3 and s₁=−56/3.
choices.feedback: The no-work condition is w₂≥Rw₁(1+2β). At R=3 the interior solution becomes feasible, but the worker still borrows.

questions.explanation: While s₁=0 and current leisure is interior, ln c₁+ln l₁ with c₁=2(12−l₁)+b gives l₁=(24+b)/4 and c₁=(24+b)/2. Current work reaches zero at b=24. For 24≤b≤60, l₁=12, c₁=b and future choices remain l₂=6,c₂=60. The saving derivative is 1/60−1/b≤0, becoming zero at b=60. For 60<b≤180, l₁=12 while future leisure remains interior: c₁=c₂=(b+60)/2, l₂=(b+60)/20 and s₁=(b−60)/2>0. At b=180, future leisure also reaches 12. questions.explanation: For a≥12, old-price sales are nonnegative and old profit is (12−8)(a−12)/0.5=8(a−12). Optimal gross reset profit is (a−8)²/2. Their difference is [(a−8)²−16(a−12)]/2=(a−16)²/2. A reset requires this to exceed eighteen, or |a−16|>6. Within [12,30], only a>22 qualifies. At equality retain the old price.
questions.source: Lecture 8, PDF pp19–40; Tutorial 10 QP and ANS.

questions.prompt: At the stated baseline, which expectations-augmented Phillips equation follows from the supply and output-unemployment equations?

choices.feedback: Output and unemployment gaps have opposite signs, giving a negative Phillips slope.
Expected inflation and the natural unemployment benchmark are interchanged.
This uses the reciprocal of the correctly converted coefficient.
Convert the raw log-price surprise into 100 log-point inflation units after equating the two output gaps.
This leaves the coefficient in raw log-price units and loses the factor of 100.
The output-unemployment coefficient must be divided by the price-surprise coefficient before conversion.

questions.explanation: Equating the gaps gives 1000(p−pᵉ)=−4(u−5). Multiply by 100/1000 to obtain π−πᵉ=−0.4(u−5). With πᵉ=2, the relation is π=2−0.4(u−5).
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51.

questions.prompt: Reset to baseline with πᵉ=2,u*=5 and h=0.4. A demand contraction gives actual u=7. What inflation and output are implied?

choices.feedback: Minus 0.8 is the inflation surprise, not actual inflation.

choices.text: π=1.6 and Y=96
choices.feedback: The actual gap is two points, not one.

choices.text: π=1.2 and Y=92
choices.feedback: The two-point positive unemployment gap reduces inflation by 0.8 and output by eight.
These signs describe unemployment below rather than above its natural rate.

choices.text: π=1.2 and Y=98
choices.feedback: The output gap is −4 times the unemployment gap, not minus the gap alone.

choices.text: π=2 and Y=100
choices.feedback: These would require actual unemployment to equal five.

questions.explanation: The cyclical gap is 7−5=2. Inflation is 2−0.4×2=1.2. Output is 100−4×2=92. Positive inflation can coexist with an adverse surprise and a negative output gap.
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51.

questions.prompt: A separate supply disturbance changes Y* to 94,u* to 6 and the raw-log supply coefficient from 1000 to 500. Expected inflation becomes 3. Demand policy maintains observed unemployment at its old level u=5. Which new (h,Y,π) and interpretation follow?

choices.text: (0.008,98,3.008); the coefficient needs no log-unit conversion
choices.feedback: Inflation is in 100 log-point units, requiring multiplication by 100.

choices.text: (0.8,98,3.8); output is below its old level but above its new potential
choices.feedback: The supply coefficient change doubles h and the new unemployment gap is negative one.

choices.text: (0.4,98,3.4); the Phillips slope stays fixed
choices.feedback: The raw-log supply coefficient changed, so its derived Phillips coefficient also changes.

choices.text: (0.8,94,3); unchanged observed unemployment means no cyclical gap
choices.feedback: The natural rate is now six, so observed five lies below the current benchmark.

choices.text: (0.8,90,2.2); output and inflation surprises are negative
choices.feedback: A negative unemployment gap corresponds to positive output and inflation surprises.

choices.text: (0.8,100,3.8); keeping u at five must keep output at 100
choices.feedback: The mapping is relative to the changed Y*=94 and u*=6.

questions.explanation: The new h is 100×4/500=0.8. Actual u=5 gives gap −1, so Y=94−4(−1)=98 and π=3−0.8(−1)=3.8. Observed output has fallen from 100 to 98, but its gap relative to new potential is +4. LRPC moves to six and SRPC becomes steeper in absolute value.
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51.

questions.prompt: Keep the disturbed structure Y*=94,u*=6,h=0.8 from the previous stated supply state. Actual inflation is sustained at 3.8 and is now fully correctly expected. Which (u,Y) follows, and which effect persists?

choices.text: u=6,Y=94; the structural shift persists while the surprise-driven excess output disappears
choices.feedback: Correct expectations set the cyclical gap to zero against the new natural benchmark.

choices.text: u=5,Y=98; repeating inflation 3.8 preserves the old surprise
choices.feedback: Once 3.8 is expected, it no longer exceeds the forecast.

choices.text: u=5,Y=100; all real changes disappear with expectation adjustment
choices.feedback: The supply and natural-rate changes are separate from the nominal surprise.

choices.text: u=6,Y=100; natural unemployment fixes the old output benchmark
choices.feedback: Natural unemployment now corresponds to the stated new potential 94.

choices.text: u=7,Y=90; correct expectations necessarily produce unemployment above natural
choices.feedback: When actual and expected inflation coincide, the equation requires a zero gap.

choices.text: u=0,Y=118; any positive sustained inflation eliminates unemployment
choices.feedback: Anticipated inflation cannot generate a permanent surprise in this baseline.

questions.explanation: The equation is 3.8=3.8−0.8(u−6), so u=6. The output-unemployment relation then gives Y=94. The prior positive output gap disappears as expectations adjust, but the stated capacity and natural-rate shifts are real structural assumptions and remain in place.
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51.

questions.prompt: Reset to Y*=100,u*=5,h=0.4. Before outcomes are known, inflation is 1 with probability 1/3 and 4 with probability 2/3. Expected inflation is the probability-weighted mean. Which expected inflation, low-state unemployment, high-state unemployment and mean unemployment follow?

choices.feedback: This takes an unweighted mean even though the probabilities differ.
Rational conditional expectations do not remove each realized forecast error.
The low-inflation state has higher, not lower, unemployment.
The most likely outcome is not the probability-weighted expectation.
The final number uses equal state weights instead of one third and two thirds.
The realized surprises differ across states, but their correctly weighted mean is zero.

questions.explanation: The mean is πᵉ=(1/3)1+(2/3)4=3. In the low state, u=5−(1−3)/0.4=10. In the high state, u=5−(4−3)/0.4=2.5. Their mean is (1/3)10+(2/3)2.5=5. Realized unemployment differs, but expected cyclical unemployment is zero in this linear illustration.
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51. Lecture 7, PDF pp14 and 34–35.

questions.prompt: Reset the starting natural rate to five. Stipulate u*next=u*current+0.25max(u−u*current,0). Actual unemployment is seven in periods 0 and 1. In period 2 it returns to five, with πᵉ=2 and h=0.4. Which period-2 natural rate and inflation follow?

choices.text: u*=5 and π=2
choices.feedback: This assumes the temporary recession left no persistent natural-rate effect.
This omits the update after period 1.
Actual unemployment below the updated natural rate implies a positive inflation surprise.

choices.text: u*=5.875 and π=2 because observed unemployment returned to its original level
choices.feedback: The relevant current benchmark is no longer five.
The second update uses the already changed natural rate, and returning actual unemployment to five does not erase the persistence.

choices.text: u*=6 and π=2.4
choices.feedback: This incorrectly applies the original two-point gap in both updates.

questions.explanation: After period 0, u*=5+0.25(7−5)=5.5. After period 1, it is 5.5+0.25(7−5.5)=5.875. Period-2 cyclical unemployment is 5−5.875=−0.875, so π=2−0.4(−0.875)=2.35. The update is explicitly stipulated to illustrate hysteresis rather than claimed as a lecture-estimated law.
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51.

questions.prompt: Separate policy design. Actual unemployment is targeted at five. All combinations πᵉ∈[2,3],u*∈[4,6],h∈[0.4,0.8] are possible. A structural reform reduces every possible u* by the same δ, with 0≤δ≤1, without changing the other ranges. What smallest δ guarantees π≤3.4 for every admissible combination?

choices.feedback: This is sufficient but is larger than the smallest required reform.
This uses a favorable coefficient or omits part of the possible natural-rate gap.

choices.text: No δ in the stated range can guarantee the ceiling
choices.feedback: At δ=0.5 the maximum is exactly 3.4, and larger reforms also meet it.
At the limiting target the worst case is πᵉ=3,h=0.8 and the highest reformed natural rate 6−δ.
Without reform the worst case gives 3+0.8(6−5)=3.8.
The worst case would still give 3+0.8(0.75)=3.6.

questions.explanation: For the smallest candidate reform, actual u=5 remains below the highest possible u*=6−δ. Inflation is therefore largest at expectation three, slope 0.8 and natural rate 6−δ. Require 3+0.8(1−δ)≤3.4, giving δ≥0.5. At δ=0.5 all other combinations give no higher inflation. Any smaller δ fails at those same admissible worst-case parameters.
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51.

questions.prompt: New calibration. Keep Y*=100 and Y−100=−4(u−u*), but let the supply coefficient b and natural rate u* be unknown constants. Two observations on one unchanged Phillips curve are (u,π)=(4,3) and (8,1). A valid independent survey gives πᵉ=2.5. Which (h,b,u*) is identified, and what happens if actual inflation 3 later becomes correctly expected with this structure fixed?

choices.text: (2,200,5); correctly expected inflation gives u=5
choices.feedback: The slope magnitude is 2/4=0.5, not its reciprocal.

choices.text: The observations identify neither h nor b even with the survey
choices.feedback: Their slope identifies h, and the supplied Okun coefficient fixes the mapping to b.
The observed slope identifies h, unit conversion identifies b, and the independent forecast separates u* from the intercept.

choices.text: (0.4,1000,5); correctly expected inflation keeps u=4
choices.feedback: This retains the old slope despite new observations and preserves a surprise after it has vanished.

choices.text: (0.5,800,4); correctly expected inflation gives u=4
choices.feedback: The first observed unemployment rate need not equal the natural rate.

choices.text: (0.5,8,5); correctly expected inflation gives u=5
choices.feedback: The b conversion loses the factor of 100 between raw log prices and the reported inflation units.

questions.explanation: The curve slope is (1−3)/(8−4)=−0.5, so h=0.5. Since h=100×4/b, b=800. The first point gives 3=2.5−0.5(4−u*), yielding u*=5. If actual and expected inflation both become three, the gap is zero, so u=5 and the output relation gives Y=100. The original baseline slope cannot be assumed after independently identifying a different one.
questions.source: Lecture 9, PDF pp14–44 and 46–51.
